title: Northrop Corp. v. Litronic Industries
summary: Predicting Illinois law, the court knocked out conflicting warranty terms and used the Code’s default, despite preferring a different interpretive approach.
notes:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1994).

Source precision: printed p. 291 cites § 2-309 and § 2-601(1) while describing a reasonable-time rejection default. That citation and description are preserved as the excerpt’s wording, not silently corrected or expanded into a full account of rejection, revocation, and warranty law. The assigned SEL text should be consulted for a provision-by-provision check. The notes examine fairness, drafting choices, master agreements, and the dangers of treating all boilerplate as deliberately negotiated.

sections.Parties: Northrop, the buyer of printed wire boards, disputed Litronic’s refusal to accept the return of allegedly defective boards.
sections.Material Facts: Litronic’s offer limited its warranty to ninety days and excluded other warranties. Northrop’s response supplied a warranty unlimited in duration. Northrop rejected boards after more than ninety days; the testing needed to discover defects was complex. The magistrate judge treated the six-month interval as reasonable under the applicable default.
sections.Procedural History: Judgment was entered for Northrop. On Litronic’s appeal, the Seventh Circuit affirmed while predicting the rule Illinois would adopt.
sections.Issue: What does § 2-207 do with terms that differ from, rather than merely add to, an offer, given that subsection (2) does not expressly repeat “different”?
sections.Holding: The court applied the knockout rule: conflicting terms in both forms dropped out and a Code default supplied the resulting term. Northrop’s unlimited warranty did not simply become the contract’s warranty.
sections.Reasoning: The opinion canvasses three approaches: knock out both conflicting terms; discard only the offeree’s different term; or treat different terms like additional terms and ask about materiality. It favors the third in principle but predicts that Illinois would follow the first, the majority approach, based on its tendencies and the Code’s interest in uniformity. Under either minority approach discussed, Litronic’s ninety-day limitation would control on these facts. The appellate role of predicting state law therefore matters to the outcome.

sections.Parties: Northrop bought electronic boards from Litronic.
sections.Material Facts: Litronic offered a 90-day warranty; Northrop’s form had no time limit. Northrop returned three boards five or six months after delivery.
sections.Procedural History: A magistrate judge awarded Northrop $58,000 for those boards and denied recovery on another transaction. Both parties appealed. The Seventh Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Which warranty terms governed despite the conflicting forms?
sections.Holding: Predicting Illinois law, the court removed both conflicting terms and applied a reasonable-duration standard.
sections.Reasoning: Northrop’s acceptance was not expressly conditional. The majority-rule prediction controlled despite Posner’s preference for treating different terms as additional terms. Ripple concurred in the result and prediction. Northrop’s separate appeal failed because it did not account for the other boards.
